title: Relationships
hook: 20 languages can carry the training; one trust miss can make Theodore's candor ring hollow.
counterintuition: Trust is not the soft part before the tools. It is the load-bearing routine that lets later candor land without sounding like power in a nicer coat.
tryThisNow: Read aloud one request for candor for 5 minutes. Watch whether it asks you to receive first, then write down the first power signal you hear.
keyTakeaway: Relationships are not warm-up talk. They are trust routines that make later candor bearable: stay centered, notice strain, build visible proof, and get before you give.

breakdown.fastRead:
20 languages can carry a method across offices, but Theodore still loses the moment if Lucy hears advice before she sees him receive truth. Radical Candor LLC is described as a global executive education company; its page says the work has been translated into 20 languages. That scale matters because the first tool cannot depend on one office mood.

Relationships opens Part 2, the tools and techniques section. It starts with trust routines: repeatable acts that show power is not the only force in the link. The order matters. Stay centered. Notice when strain keeps you from showing up well. Ask what direct reports can observe when you build trust. Then receive before you advise: seek criticism before handing it out. If Theodore skips that order, every later script charges trust he has not paid into.
breakdown.deepRead:
Receiving first lowers the price of honesty. When a boss asks for hard truth before giving it, the other person sees that candor is not a one-way toll. Every advice-first habit charges trust before anyone has a chance to earn it.

Project lead Theodore wants to help analyst Lucy, and his first draft starts with advice. Then the Relationships prompts slow him down. They ask what keeps him centered, when strain had made him reactive, and which visible acts let direct reports trust him. Those are not private diary questions. They name the places where strain leaks into behavior.

Aurelie, a department head, feels the same cost. She can ask for candor only after she has shown how she handles strain. If she snaps, then asks for openness, she has made the hard truth more expensive. Ask first, then advise.

Order of Operations is the official sequence across Chapters 5-6: solicit feedback, give feedback to individuals, then encourage it among peers. Relationships uses the first move as relationship work. Get before you give means Theodore asks what Lucy sees in him before he tells her what he sees in her.

Who pays when the first trust signal appears only after the fight? Lucy does. She has to risk the truth while Theodore keeps the safer role. Price the trust signal before you ask for candor. If the price all lands on the person with less power, the routine has not begun.
breakdown.fullRead:
Lisa's training note gives the scale without making scale the lesson. That page also notes a 20-language reach. The useful point is not size. It is that a relationship practice has to travel as behavior, not as a local custom. That is why Lisa keeps the repeated ask and cuts the local custom before it hardens.

The chronology is spare. Part 2 begins with Relationships. That unit asks you to name activities that keep you centered. It asks when you could not bring your best self to work. It asks how trust is built with direct reports. Then the order across Chapters 5-6 begins with soliciting feedback. The pressure rises only after that.

That order reverses the move many people make under stress. You feel a miss, so you reach for a script, a sharper line, or a formal tool. But relationship work comes before Guidance, Team, and Results because those later tools carry more heat. Crisis is a poor time to build the first proof of trust.

What has Theodore done that makes hard truth less costly for Lucy? If the answer is nothing, his next sentence should not be advice. It should be a request he can bear to hear answered. Small counts here. A steady pause before reply. A real question about his conduct. A visible change when the answer hurts.

The limit matters. If Lucy needs a clear standard now, Theodore cannot hide inside endless listening. Trust routines are not delay tactics. They break when the person with power keeps asking for feelings but never makes a hard call. In that case, the cost has merely moved, and Lucy still pays it.

You can use the move without a title. Before you correct a partner, a volunteer, or a classmate, ask whether you have made truth safe in both directions. If you have not, receive first. If you already asked and did nothing with the answer, do not ask again as theater. Change one visible behavior.

That is why the training context belongs here. A company can teach a routine; it cannot teach chemistry on command. Translation into 20 languages points to the portable piece: stay centered, invite criticism upward, and build trust through repeated proof. Not charm. Not rank. Proof.

Theodore does not need a grand confession. He needs to lower the cost of Lucy's next true sentence. He can name the strain that makes him defensive, ask where it shows up, and make one change she can see. Receiving first is not a slogan here. It is the first receipt.

examples.title: The Ask Comes Late

planSpec.requiredBeat: trace the late ask back to who received first

examples.scenario: After the Friday handoff on the support floor, project lead Theodore traced the miss after his direct report stopped adding facts. He had ignored the Order of Operations: solicit feedback, then give it. One object was left from the earlier exchange. A cold mug sat beside him. He called back and used get before give, asking what he made harder to say. The answer had not arrived when the call ended.
examples.whatToDo: Theodore asks for one hard truth before any advice.

examples.title: The Delay Lands

planSpec.requiredBeat: name the centering act before the reply

examples.scenario: During a Monday staffing call in operations, department head Aurelie first made the effect visible when she delayed a sharp reply. Before the prompt, strain became speed, and the speed sounded like blame. After it, Aurelie named the activity that helped her stay centered and said build trust with direct reports had to include her own pause. "I wanted to react," Aurelie said. "I chose to come back steadier." A hard fact came back.
examples.whatToDo: Aurelie gives you the command: name the act that steadies you before you ask another person for candor.
examples.whyItMatters: Aurelie makes the other person pay less when she carries her own strain first.

examples.title: The Custom Almost Travels

planSpec.requiredBeat: redesign the exercise so portable behavior replaces local custom

examples.scenario: In facilitator prep for a training cohort, Lisa rewrites the first exercise before the slides lock. The draft treats Radical Candor LLC, a global executive education company, as if relationships were private chemistry from one office culture. The official page says the work has been translated into 20 languages, so she replaces the local ritual with one repeatable ask: what have you done that makes truth safer to give you?
examples.whatToDo: Lisa keeps the 20-language clue in view: preserve the behavior that can be practiced twice, not the office custom that happened to carry it once.
examples.whyItMatters: The redesign makes the routine teachable. Relationship trust has to travel as an observable act, because chemistry cannot scale on command.

examples.title: The Standard Is Earned

planSpec.requiredBeat: test a trust claim against observable direct-report evidence

examples.scenario: During a project-group trust check, Lucy tests Theodore's claim against what direct reports can actually observe. His intent sounds clear to him because the title is his; it does not lower the risk for her. The standard is build trust through evidence, not assumption. Until Theodore names a practice she can see twice, the claim remains only a promise from the person with more power.
examples.whatToDo: Make trust observable. Name the practice another person can see, then repeat it before asking them to risk a sharper truth.
examples.whyItMatters: Theodore cannot borrow trust from his title. Repeated evidence is the move that lowers the risk for the direct report.

examples.title: The Advice Gets Deleted

planSpec.requiredBeat: delete the advice until the ask comes first

examples.scenario: Why is Theodore deleting the advice he already wrote? Because the Order of Operations starts when he solicits feedback, and get before give means the first move is to receive. He is cutting the first line now. The cursor blinks at the start of his note. He changes "Here is what you should do" to "What am I missing in how I handle this?" A hard truth comes back. He waits to advise until he has heard it.
examples.whatToDo: Theodore answers the reader's worry: yes, the cost is waiting; ask upward before giving counsel.
examples.whyItMatters: The other person can test whether candor is reciprocal. The delay buys trust that a fast answer would spend.

examples.title: The Strain Gets Named
examples.scenario: At the check-in itself, Aurelie answered for the commitment she had made. She had promised to stay centered by naming the moment when she could not bring her best self to work. The first answer blamed pressure. The miss was close. Then she named the real pattern: when strained, she answered too fast. Lisa asked for the safeguard before direct reports felt the cost.
examples.whatToDo: Aurelie names one failure point before blame.
examples.whyItMatters: Lisa gets a safeguard, not a mood report.

questions.prompt: Several actions look useful at the start of a tools section when a new lead wants better candor after a guarded exchange. Which comes first, and why?
choices: Start by earning trust through a repeatable relationship habit, because later feedback can only carry what that habit has made credible.
Start by selecting a stronger script for the difficult talk, because cleaner wording can make missing trust less visible when strain rises.
Start by asking the most senior person which tactic to use, because rank can stand in for relationship proof when the habit is weak.
questions.explanation: The first tool is trust-building behavior. The script answer tempts because wording matters, but scripts still fail when trust is absent.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood volunteer group wants to borrow this move after members say the tone depends on who shows up. What maps best from the training context?
choices: Let the warmest member set the tone for every hard exchange, because relationship skill depends mainly on personal chemistry.
Turn trust into a repeatable habit the group can practice, because the training context treats relationships as teachable behavior.
Ask a respected outside brand to settle the standard for the group, because borrowed standing can replace local trust.
questions.explanation: The training context points to routines that can be taught. Warm chemistry is close enough to sound kind, but this move rejects chemistry as the core tool.

questions.prompt: The rollout already failed: candor appeared only after conflict got hot, and the first trust signal came under pressure. What earlier step caused the miss?
choices: They used too few talk tracks, so pressure rose because the later words were not carefully chosen for the hardest exchange.
They chose the wrong later tool, even though a trust base had already been built before pressure rose and stayed visible.
They waited for a performance problem before building the first trust signal, so conflict arrived before capacity.
questions.explanation: The cause is late trust-building. The talk-track answer is plausible, but it treats wording as the gap when timing caused the failure.

questions.prompt: Before a supervisor asks a direct report to accept hard input after weeks of guarded answers, which priority fits the order taught here?
choices: Give the direct report the hard input first, because seeing the standard early will make later upward candor easier for both sides.
Set peers up to exchange criticism first, because sideways candor removes the pressure from the supervisor's role before she receives any.
Ask what the supervisor needs to hear about her own behavior, because receiving first makes candor reciprocal.
questions.explanation: The sequence begins with soliciting feedback. Peer exchange is a real later move, but using it first skips the power-lowering act.

questions.prompt: A supervisor keeps giving careful advice after every update, yet the sharp fact stays hidden and the relationship feels polite but thin. What is actually wrong?
choices: He offers counsel before proving he can hear hard truth, so the exchange still runs one way.
He asks for too much candor from below, so he should return to advice until others trust his expertise.
He lacks a formal title for the exchange, so a role label should create the permission his behavior has not earned.
questions.explanation: Get before give means he must receive first. Waiting to ask for candor sounds safer, but it keeps power moving one way.

questions.prompt: At a school club, an older student wants younger members to speak honestly after a tense practice. What maps from this move?
choices: Give repeated, visible proof that honesty is safe, because power makes trust something the older student must earn.
Assume the younger members trust the older student by default, because shared club membership creates enough safety.
Aim the trust routine at the club handbook, because the written rule can carry what the older student has not shown.
questions.explanation: The power gap makes evidence necessary. The handbook answer borrows the right idea of proof but aims it at a document instead of behavior.

questions.prompt: A supervisor snaps twice, then asks for candor and gets guarded answers from people with less power. Which repair starts closest to the cause?
choices: Treat composure as a private wellness matter and keep it separate from how others decide whether to trust her.
Name one activity that keeps her centered before the next hard exchange, because her state affects the relationship.
Ask the direct report to be more resilient during tense exchanges, because that person can absorb strain while trust develops.
questions.explanation: Centering is relationship protection, not private decoration. Asking the other person to absorb strain moves the cost downward.

questions.prompt: A volunteer adapts the routine for a club with a different culture. What should she preserve?
choices: Copy the original office custom closely, because the known scene has already carried the method elsewhere.
Let the local status order decide who may speak first, because translation means each culture supplies the trust signal.
Keep the behavior small and portable, because the useful piece is repeated trust behavior rather than one office style.
questions.explanation: The 20-language fact points to portable behavior. Copying the office custom feels faithful, but it mistakes one setting for the mechanism.

questions.prompt: A supervisor's last attempt failed after strain leaked into her answer and the other person stopped being candid. Which earlier omission best explains it?
choices: She invited upward criticism too early, so the act of receiving made the pressure worse.
She never named the predictable strain that makes her react, so no safeguard existed when it returned.
She used a routine instead of trusting personal steadiness, so the process created distance during the hard exchange.
questions.explanation: The missing step is self-awareness about the failure point. The routine answer sounds human, but routines protect against strain.

reviewCards.front: When a tools section begins, what should come before scripts?
reviewCards.back: Build trust through a repeatable relationship habit. Later candor can only carry the strain that the relationship has capacity to bear.

reviewCards.front: What does get before you give require?
reviewCards.back: Ask for criticism about your own behavior before offering correction. Receiving first lowers hierarchy and makes candor reciprocal.

reviewCards.front: Why does staying centered belong in relationship work?
reviewCards.back: Your state is not private once it shapes how others experience your power. A centering habit keeps strain from becoming defensiveness.

reviewCards.front: What does a bad-day prompt reveal?
reviewCards.back: It names the pattern that makes you less able to bring your best self to work. Once named, the pattern can get a safeguard.

reviewCards.front: How do direct reports learn to trust you?
reviewCards.back: Through repeated evidence they can observe. Intentions and titles are too cheap; the other person needs proof that shows up in behavior.

reviewCards.front: Why does the 20-language fact matter for practice?
reviewCards.back: It points away from copying one culture. The portable piece is a behavior people can repeat: receive first, stay centered, and build visible trust.

reviewCards.front: Why not wait until a performance problem appears?
reviewCards.back: Pressure makes first trust signals harder to believe. Build the relationship capacity before later tools raise the stakes.

implementationPlan.title: Price The Trust Signal
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Price The Trust Signal. Before you ask for candor, name the behavior that makes your ask less costly to answer. If the price is all on the other person, receive first and make the promise smaller. Trust grows through proof another person can see.

ifThenPlans.context: You want to offer advice to someone with less power.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I want to offer advice to someone with less power, then I count 1 criticism I have requested about my own behavior and ask it before advising.

ifThenPlans.context: You feel strained before a hard exchange.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I feel strained before a hard exchange, then I measure 5 minutes of centering before I reply.

ifThenPlans.context: A trust claim sounds too broad.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a trust claim sounds too broad, then I count 1 visible behavior that would prove it this week.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Replace one advice-first reply with a 10-minute read-aloud request: ask for one hard truth about your own behavior before you offer any counsel.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For 10 minutes each Friday, say aloud: "I asked for hard truth before I advised. I stayed centered by __. I showed trust by __." Write the blank you missed most.

memorableLines.text: Every advice-first habit charges trust before anyone has a chance to earn it.
memorableLines.why: Names the concrete price of advising before receiving.

memorableLines.text: What has Theodore done that makes hard truth less costly for Lucy?
memorableLines.why: Turns relationship capacity into a question the reader can apply.

memorableLines.text: Price the trust signal before you ask for candor.
memorableLines.why: Carries the chapter's central image as a short command.
